parts.name: Broadaxe
parts.desc: A single deep edge that cuts further into a rim than any stock blade and hands most of the shock straight back up the shaft.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is cleaver. Sharp 1.00 goes to 1.26, which is 26 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling, and taken 1.22 goes to 1.46 to pay for it; mass and radius are held at cleaver's values so the trade reads cleanly against it. Measured on fixed chassis the sharp gain is worth roughly 8 win points and the recoil costs roughly 10, which is why it audits at 44.4 pull against cleaver's 49.1 with a lower ceiling too.

parts.name: Chisel
parts.desc: Every gram is gathered into one narrow point, so it cuts deeper than anything in the stock box and has almost no rim left to carry it.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is cleaver. Sharp 1.30 is 30 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling; radius 0.0188 is 8 percent under the Tier 1 floor, which costs both contact reach and moment of inertia and therefore raises spin decay. Radius is the most expensive stat in the slot at about 1.5 win points per millimetre, so a small nominal move on it pays for a large one on sharp. Pull 45.0 against cleaver 49.1.

parts.name: Millstone
parts.desc: A short heavy stone of a wheel that shoulders other tops aside and gives up its reach to do it.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is bulwark. Mass 0.0224 is 22 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and radius 0.0188 is 8 percent under the Tier 1 floor, which is the brief's own rule that a big number costs real metal or real reach. This is the tightest margin in the set at plus 3.3 pull over bulwark, so re audit it after any change to massCost, inertiaPow or the defense archetype.

parts.name: Ploughshare
parts.desc: The heaviest plate the mount will carry, ground smooth so it shoves tops off their line instead of cutting them.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is anvil. Mass 0.0242 is 32 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling, paid with sharp 0.14, which is 22 percent under the Tier 1 floor and costs about twice what the mass buys, since sharp feeds both the normal impulse and the shock drain. Pull 34.6 against anvil 44.1, so it is a heavy blade that genuinely cannot finish anyone.

parts.name: Cartwheel
parts.desc: The widest ring the mount will hold, rolled thin and left blunt, so it carries spin for a very long time and can barely mark anything.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is halo. Radius 0.0262 is the stated mount limit, so a 25 percent push is physically impossible here and the cap itself is the extreme; this is the widest blade the game can ever have and the only part in my set that meets the Flywheel rig threshold. Sharp 0.12 is 33 percent under the Tier 1 floor and pays for it. Pull 37.2 against halo 40.6.

parts.name: Bolster
parts.desc: A packed rim that swallows a hit instead of returning it, with no edge left to answer one.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is orbit. Rest 0.18 is 31 percent under the Tier 1 floor, so contact dies inside the blade rather than throwing either top clear, and sharp 0.10 is 44 percent under the floor to pay for it. Taken sits at 0.62, deliberately just above the Tier 1 floor: an earlier draft pushed taken to 0.44 and, with mass, radius and sharp all at their floors, it still pulled 7 points over its sibling and set a new ceiling for the whole slot. See the note on taken.

parts.name: Rasp
parts.desc: A file rather than a knife, it grips a passing rim and drags the spin off it instead of throwing it clear.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is sabre. Gear 1.82 is 30 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and rest 0.16 is 38 percent under the Tier 1 floor, so it holds contact rather than breaking it, which is the whole point of a toothed rim. Pull 41.8 against sabre 44.1. Read the note on gear before tuning this one: it is currently the cheapest push in the slot because the tangential impulse is clamped in over half of all contacts.

parts.name: Hailstone
parts.desc: Hard and polished, it kicks away from every contact it makes and never grips long enough to trade spin.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is crest. Rest 1.20 is 26 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and gear 0.14 is 44 percent under the Tier 1 floor. Restitution is the slot's one genuine matchup stat: measured on a fixed chassis, high rest gains about 8 points against a same spinning opponent and loses about 5 against an opposite spinning one, because breaking contact early saves you from a scrub and robs you of a mesh. Pull 47.0 against crest 45.0.

parts.name: Shrike
parts.desc: The deepest edge ever fitted to a mount, hung on a blade so light and thin that it begins to give once the spin is gone.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is cleaver. Sharp 1.62 is 62 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and is the single most extreme number in this proposal; taken 1.52 pays 13 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and Glass doubles that again below 40 percent spin. Glass is the only drawback that reliably costs anything, measured at minus 5 to minus 11 win points on fixed chassis, so this is the one Relic where the named flaw does most of the paying. Ceiling 66.9, the highest of any attack blade in the catalogue, and pull 39.4 against cleaver 49.1: exactly the shape a Relic should have.

parts.name: Sledge
parts.desc: A hardened face that turns one clean contact into a single enormous blow and never lands another like it.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is sabre. Rest 1.42 is 49 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling, which is what makes the opening connection huge, since lock wear scales as the cube of the impulse and One Shot triples the first strike a top lands. Taken 1.52 pays 13 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and carries the whole price, because One Shot measured as a net positive of plus 0.9 to plus 2.1 win points rather than a cost. Pull 40.2 against sabre 44.1.

parts.name: Ingot
parts.desc: A dense billet with barely any rim to it, slow to get moving and then very hard to move.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is bulwark. Mass 0.0250 is 36 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and is the heaviest blade in the game; the payment is radius 0.0206 pinned to the very bottom of the Tier 1 band, which is where all the cost lives because radius drives both inertia and contact reach, plus taken 1.06, which is high for a defensive blade because a billet with no rim rings the shock straight into the lock. Cold Start measured at 0 to minus 3.5. Pull 38.9 against bulwark 36.0, the second tightest margin in the set.

parts.name: Hookbill
parts.desc: A rim cut into meshing teeth that tears spin off whatever it touches and burns through its own doing it.
parts.rationale: Tier 1 sibling is halo. Gear 2.10 is 50 percent past the Tier 1 ceiling and taken 1.08 pays for it, far above what any stamina blade carries, because a toothed rim cannot shed a hit sideways. Hungry raises the steal and the baseline decay together. Pull 41.8 against halo 40.6. Be warned that this part is balanced on its other stats and not on gear, because gear is close to inert today: see the note on jtCap.

notes:
HOW THIS WAS VERIFIED. I edited no repo file. I copied src/sim2.js and tools/partaudit.js into a scratch directory, appended the twelve blades to the copy, and restricted the audit to the blade slot. Files kept at /tmp/claude-1000/-workspaces-lucid-winds/20a4fdff-a3a0-46de-8c48-50f49653330c/scratchpad/blade-stream (props.json, sim_blade.js, bladeaudit.js, mk.py). Note the scratchpad root is shared with other streams; my work is namespaced in blade-stream. Measured against sim2.js as it stood at 08:20 today, which already carries your drawback plumbing, the rig table and applyMods.

RESULT. PART AUDIT OK at both settings. Defaults, node partaudit 8 2 40: blade ceiling spread 21.9, identical to the Tier 1 only baseline of 21.9, pull spread 17.2, no creep flags. Higher resolution, 20 4 90: ceiling spread 22.5, pull spread 14.5, no creep flags. Every Tier 2 and Tier 3 part sits below its sibling plus 4 at both settings. Tightest margins, both at high resolution: millstone plus 3.3 over bulwark and ingot plus 2.9 over bulwark. Everything else is at or below plus 2.0, and seven of the twelve are net negative on pull. The three parts with a ceiling above their sibling's are shrike, bolster and ploughshare, which is the Relic and near Relic shape the brief asks for.

FOUR MEASURED FACTS THAT DROVE THE NUMBERS.

1. The six stats are wildly unequal, so a flat 25 percent rule cannot be applied evenly. Swept one at a time on a fixed crest like blade over 140 shells against the four archetype gauntlet: sharp is worth about 33 win points per 1.00, taken about minus 40 per 1.00 in its working band, mass about 1.05 points per 0.001 kg, radius about 1.05 points per 0.001 m rising to 1.8 near the floor, and gear and rest are within noise of flat on the mean. So I paired heavyweight pushes with heavyweight payments (sharp with taken), midweight with midweight (mass with radius), and featherweight with featherweight (gear with rest). Every push exits the Tier 1 range by 22 to 62 percent or hits the stated mount limit; where the paid stat's nominal percentage is smaller than the push, its measured win rate cost is larger, which is the honest reading of paying for it.

2. Taken cannot be pushed below its Tier 1 floor of 0.60. A draft Bolster at taken 0.44 with mass, radius and sharp all at their floors still pulled plus 7.2 over orbit and set a ceiling of 79.7, well outside the whole catalogue. Taken is the slot's price and not one of its products, which matches your own line that sharpness and restitution are paid for in taken. No part in this proposal pushes it.

3. Radius is capped by the mount at 0.0262, so a 25 percent push on it does not exist. Cartwheel takes it to the cap and pays in sharp. The other direction is available but brutal: radius 25 percent under the floor would be 0.0153, worth about minus 20 win points, so my radius payments are 0.0188 to 0.0206, small in percent and large in effect.

4. Gear is close to inert. In 60,191 sampled contacts the tangential impulse was clamped at jtCap in 53.7 percent of them, so the rim friction coefficient does not express itself for over half of all hits. Sweeping gear from 0.10 to 2.10 moved the win rate by under 2 points in either spin direction. Rasp at 1.82 and Hookbill at 2.10 are therefore balanced on their other stats. If you raise jtCap or lower muMax to make spin stealing legible, re audit those two first, and expect Hookbill to move most because Hungry multiplies gear again.

DRAWBACK PRICES, measured on your live implementation, three fixed blades, 140 shells each. Glass minus 8.4, minus 5.1, minus 10.8. Cold Start plus 0.1, minus 3.1, minus 3.5. Greedy minus 1.2, minus 1.4, minus 2.6. Loose Lock plus 0.5, minus 3.7, plus 2.5. Hungry plus 0.5, plus 1.3, minus 0.3. One Shot plus 2.1, plus 1.9, plus 0.9. Only Glass is reliably expensive; Hungry and One Shot are net positives as written, and Loose Lock is a gain on a heavy chassis because the stable bonus outweighs the halved burst resist. That is why Shrike is the only Relic whose flaw carries the price and the other three pay in stats. If you want the drawbacks to bite, One Shot is the one to look at: the follow up penalty of 0.4 barely registers because bursts are rare, so the triple on the first strike is close to free.

NO NEW DRAWBACKS. I used four of the six named ones and needed neither of my two allowances. Greedy and Loose Lock read as core and ratchet flaws rather than blade flaws, so I left them to those streams.

ONE FRAGILITY IN THE GATE, not in the parts. The sibling is the Tier 1 part in the same role with the nearest ceiling, and ties resolve by BLADES array order. Attack has sabre at 46.4 pull and shard at 35.8 sitting on the same ceiling in the default run, so a part landing between them is scored against whichever the array lists first. Two of my drafts sat on that exact tie before I moved them clear. If the blade list is reordered, or if a Tier 2 blade from another stream lands near those ceilings, re run the audit rather than trusting the last green.

RIG INTERACTIONS, for whoever writes the rig table. Cartwheel at 0.0262 is the only part here that meets the Flywheel radius threshold of 0.024. Broadaxe, Chisel, Rasp, Shrike and Sledge all clear the Hammer threshold of sharp 0.85, and Rasp is the only one that also wants a high gearMul assist, so Rasp plus a hook or rake assist is where Spin Thief and Rail Lock will stack. Sledge at rest 1.42 plus a bevelled assist is the burst build to watch, because wear goes as the cube of the impulse and One Shot triples the first one.

ALL TWELVE IDS ARE NEW and do not collide with any existing id in any slot. Names are workshop, weather, tool, bird and mineral words with no branded or licensed content. No copy contains a dash or a hyphen. Numbers are exact as given; please do not round them, because the two tightest parts have under one point of headroom.
